newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hesse vote gives Kohl much-needed boost.
newsitem.headline: Hesse vote gives Kohl much-needed boost.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), struggling in national voter surveys against a backdrop of record unemployment, received a badly-needed boost in local elections on Sunday.

Its vote in the state of Hesse rose one percentage point to 33.0 percent and it gained 2.9 points to 36.3 percent in the country's financial capital of Frankfurt, long a bastion of the left-wing Social Democrats, preliminary official results showed.

CDU officials quickly seized on the results, saying they endorsed Kohl's drive for tax and pension reforms, now the subject of heated wrangling both within his coalition and with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

"The victory in Frankfurt and the good results statewide in Hesse show that the CDU has passed the voters' test," said CDU general secretary Peter Hintze. "These elections represent an endorsement for the reform policies of Chancellor Helmut Kohl."
The Hesse election came at a difficult time for Kohl's government which has been criticised for presiding over the worst unemployment since the 1930s.
A newspaper on Sunday said February jobless data due on Thursday would show that 4.8 million people were out of work, a new postwar record.

The vote in Hesse, one of Germany's wealthiest states with 4.5 million eligible voters, was dominated by local issues but carried national implications as one of only two elections this year. Hamburg votes in September.
The SPD, the main opposition party in Bonn, also posted modest gains in Hesse, gaining 1.6 points to 38.0 percent comapred with the last local election in 1993.
"This shows we are moving forward," said Hesse premier Hans Eichel of the SPD. His party has bounced back in voter surveys after a steep plunge in 1995.
The main losers in Hesse were the smaller parties. The environmentalist Greens stagnated while the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) and far-right Republicans suffered losses.
The Greens were unchanged at 11.0 percent, the FDP dropped to 4.0 percent from 5.1 percent and the Republicans declined to 6.6 percent from 8.3 percent.
In what all parties attributed to general discontent with politics, voter turnout in warm and sunny weather dropped to 66.0 percent from 71.3 in 1993.

Kohl earlier described the Hesse poll as an important foretaste for parliamentary elections due in 1998. Opinion polls suggest his coalition with the FDP would lose its majority in the Bundestag or lower house of the federal parliament if a general election was held now.
In Frankfurt, a city of 660,000 people, the CDU recorded impressive gains owing mainly to the popularity of mayor Petra Roth.

"This result, coming a year and a half before the general elections, should help Chancellor Kohl," she said. "It shows that he can rely on Frankfurt. I'm proud that in Frankfurt the CDU was elected as a modern, big-city party."
The SPD, its image dented by years of infighting with the Greens, saw its vote fall to 29.1 percent from 32.0 percent, its worst result in Frankfurt since the war.

The Greens gained 2.9 points to 16.9 percent and the FDP, helped by their leading candidate. Ignatz Bubis, Germany's Jewish leader, entered the city's parliament for the first time in 16 years with 5.6 percent.
